body: Chilean road lines are either all white or all yellow. All white lines are most common, while all yellow lines appear in National Parks or high snowfall areas and are almost unique in the Americas.
Chile uses a unique white Google car with no antenna in Generation 3, with two variants: plain white or white with a visible black section. Generation 4 has a blue car.
Chile uses square concrete poles with indentations on both sides similar to Brazilian poles but with fewer supports. Wooden poles are also common.
Regular vehicles have white license plates, while commercial and taxi vehicles have orange plates.
Slots are often visible at the top of Chilean signposts.
Chilean bollards resemble Spanish style, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are uncommon.
Sometimes orange temporary bollards with two white stripes at the top are found in Chile.
Bridges in Chile often have red painted fence posts.
Chile spans over 4,000 km north to south, resulting in varied climates: arid deserts in the north, temperate Mediterranean in the center, and cold oceanic in the south.
Chile's road naming system uses letters from A to Y increasing from north to south.
The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth with almost no vegetation.
Arica y Parinacota features smooth, sandy mountains with eroded or bulbous shapes and common valleys.
Rocky, uneven mountains are common in the Atacama and northern Coquimbo regions.
Brownish-red soil is sometimes visible in Atacama province, especially in Generation 3 imagery.
Eucalyptus plantations combined with dry climate indicate southwestern Valparaíso.
The area around Santiago is characterized by a semi-arid climate with dry hills and scattered vegetation.
Maule province is similar to Santiago but greener with common vineyards and a Mediterranean climate.
Concepción pines with puffy needles are common in Bio Bio, less so in Ñuble and Araucania.
Narrow roads with trees lining both sides are common in Bio Bio and Araucania.
Monkey puzzle trees are found in eastern Araucania and across the border in Argentina.
Isla Grande de Chiloé features rolling agricultural landscapes similar to New Zealand.
Chilean rhubarb, recognizable by its large cabbage-like leaves, is common on Isla Grande and nearby mainland areas.
Southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén have lush green valleys with rocky mountains and often overcast skies.
Southern Aysén displays autumn colors with orange and red vegetation, though not all coverage here shows this.
Ruta A-31 is notable for its high altitude and steep drop into a northern valley, featuring Generation 3 sunset coverage.
Generation 4 sunset coverage on Ruta 21 shows a white dome near Calama and warm gradients with glowing volcano tops to the east.
More Generation 4 sunset coverage is found on B-710 and Ruta 5 with differing landscape openness; road angles assist in locating.
Ruta 1 coastal road is distinct with mountain walls to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west.
Part of Ruta 41 lies in a valley viewed with snowy mountains, trees, vineyards, and triple yellow lines.
Purple Large-leaved Lupines commonly grow along Ruta 240.
Yellow lines on concrete mark the paved section of Ruta 9 in southern Chile, characterized by barren, grassy, treeless landscapes.
Lauca National Park features snow-capped mountains and volcanoes, new smooth dark paved roads.
Northern Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve is marked by Tamarugo trees along a mediocre quality road heading northwest.
Alto Loa National Reserve has a wide open landscape with salt pans and snow-capped volcanoes but no paved roads.
Los Flamencos National Reserve shows smooth mountains with reddish tint, salt pans, and uses triple yellow lines with short dashes westward.
Nevado Tres Cruces National Park features vast salt pans, red sand, snow-capped volcanoes, and paved roads.
Llanos de Challe National Park has brown roadside dirt, light sand patches, juniper plants, dark mountains, and often overcast skies.
Alto Bio Bio National Reserve is vast, mostly treeless, with triple yellow lines, a cold high altitude feel, and monkey puzzles in the east.
Puyehue National Park has dense vegetation, triple yellow pavement lines, frequent tar snakes, and leafless dead trees to the east.
Arica features a slight sandy ridge with gradual incline.
Iquique is known for a larger, towering ridge.
Antofagasta features rockier, uneven ridges.
San Pedro de Atacama is recognizable by clay brick walls, often topped with triangles.
Lanco features orange street signs at nearly every intersection.
O'Higgins has large mountains to the east casting shadows, with snow-capped mountains visible to the west.
Orange lamps are common in Calama and Chañaral, rare elsewhere in smaller cities.
Green dome-shaped lamps are seen in Copiapó.
Lamps with photocells are common in Santiago but rare in other cities.
Talca has grey lamps with thin, flat tops and rounded undersides.
Concepción features blue rectangular lamps with yellow stripes.
Puerto Montt and Temuco have lamps with silver tops and grey bottoms.
Arica poles have white paint with black numbers, while other Atacama cities use yellow paint that may fade to white.
El Salvador features round poles painted black.
Near Santiago Zoo, a Google car tows a white and silver trailer labeled 'Outback'.
A grey Toyota Hilux with gear and snorkel appears from Baños Morales to a point where trekking continues on foot.
Conguillio National Park is marked by a white truck with side mirrors and front right antenna.
Puerto Williams, Chile’s southernmost street view town, features a white pickup truck with visible mirrors. It is remote compared to normal car coverage.
The Atacama Large Millimeter Array is recognizable by numerous radio telescopes in a barren snowy setting.
ALMA OSF features large radio telescopes and rural facilities.
A horse trekker northwest of San Filipe is seen; a similar trekker is present across the Argentinian border.
Torres del Paine is marked by sharp peaked mountains and trekkers with orange helmets walking on glaciers.
